_meta.source: JRC ASAP (Anomaly hot Spots of Agricultural Production)
_meta.notes: Current-season agricultural stress from the EC Joint Research Centre's ASAP monthly expert assessment. Latest assessment per country from the full 2016-present series; most recent date in this run 2026-09-11. hotspot_code: 0 no hotspot, 1 hotspot, 2 major hotspot. ASAP's raw hs_code 3 means NOT ASSESSED, not a severity above 2 — those countries (8 in this run) carry hotspot_code null and stress_score null. NULL IS NOT ZERO: no assessment is not an all-clear, and several unassessed countries have dozens of subnational crop warnings standing (units_crop_warning is populated regardless of code). stress_score 0-100 is banded by the JRC verdict (0-20 / 40-70 / 75-100 for codes 0/1/2) and spread within band by units_crop_warning normalised against that country's own historical maximum — so the expert verdict always dominates the ranking and the count only breaks ties. COVERAGE IS NOT GLOBAL: ASAP monitors 79 food-insecure countries only. A country absent from this payload is one ASAP does not watch (USA, Ukraine, Brazil, India, Australia among them) — absence must NOT be presented as an absence of stress. Unlike Aqueduct baseline and CCKP normals, this is a current-season signal and goes stale monthly; ASAP publishes around the 10th.

AFG.comment:
In Afghanistan, spring wheat harvest is nearing completion while rice harvest will start in October and average to above average biomass across the country suggests favourable prospects. Land preparation is underway for winter wheat and barley to be sown in October and November under very favourable rainfall conditions as a consequence of El Niño and according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.
 Afghanistan continues to face high levels of hunger with about 14 million people estimated in acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 or above) for the period April – September 2026 as a result of prolonged economic deterioration, recurrent drought, refugee returns, declining humanitarian aid and decreasing remittances according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1159816/?iso3=AFG] IPC report from 16 December 2025 and [https://www.wfp.org/emergencies/afghanistan] WFP.

AGO.comment: Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit across the entire southern and central regions, stretching up along the northern coastal strip; conversely, only the interior northern and northeastern provinces are projected to receive near-average to above-average precipitation. As reported by [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=AGO] FAO GIEWS (03/09), this dry outlook is heavily influenced by the ongoing El Niño event, which emerged in June and is typically associated with suppressed rainfall totals across much of Southern Africa. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

BDI.comment: Season A planting of crops such as sorghum, maize and beans is about to start under below-average rainfall conditions. However, Burundi is forecast to receive El Niño-related above-average rainfall during the October–December (OND) rainy season, as indicated by the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/burundi/wfp-burundi-country-brief-september-2026] WFP, the 2026B harvest improved market supplies in Burundi and prices remained broadly stable in August 2026, but most staples stayed above their five-year average, and the gradual depletion of household stocks, high inflation and fuel supply risks could weaken household access to food during the upcoming lean season.

BEN.comment: The first-season maize harvest is currently underway in the southern parts of the country and is expected to finish by the end of September. Overall prospects remain average, sustained by generally favourable, near-average cumulative rainfall during crop development. Simultaneously, planting for the second-season maize is progressing in the south under average rainfall conditions, with completion also anticipated by late September. In contrast, the northern provinces have experienced highly irregular rainfall distribution. The region suffered significant moisture deficits at the start of the season in April (with cumulative rainfall roughly 40% to 65% below-average) and again between late June and mid-July (falling 30% to 50% below average). As a result, particularly poor crop and rangeland biomass conditions are evident across northern departments. In Borgou province, specifically, nearly 55% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. The provinces of Alibori, Atakora, and Donga are similarly impacted, though to a lesser extent, with 30% to 35% of their active crop areas exhibiting vegetation stress. Persistent insecurity further exacerbates these poor northern crop and rangeland conditions. According to the [https://reliefweb.int/report/benin/wfp-benin-country-brief-august-2026] WFP (Benin Country Brief, August 2026), the resurgence of armed incidents linked to the Sahel crisis continues to worsen Benin's humanitarian situation. This instability primarily impacts the Atacora, Alibori, and Borgou departments, which are currently hosting internally displaced persons alongside refugees and asylum seekers from Burkina Faso, Niger, Togo, and Nigeria.

BFA.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 main-season maize crop is ongoing, while the sorghum and millet harvests will begin in October. The 2026 agricultural season has been severely impacted by irregular rainfall distribution, resulting in widespread moisture stress across many regions as of mid-September. This degradation is most acute within the country's central part, where poor conditions affect 50% to 70% of the active crop area across the Plateau-Central, Centre-Ouest, and Centre regions. In contrast, the northern belt (Centre-Nord, Nord) and the outer peripheries, spanning the west (Boucle du Mouhoun and Hauts-Bassins), the east (Centre-Est), and the far southwest (Sud-Ouest), are less severely hit, with a greenness anomaly impacting nearly 30% to 35% of the crop area. Pastoral conditions are mirroring these conditions; while pasture regeneration and water point replenishment are progressively improving nationwide ([https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Z6ICni6evYo_XEyw8_S_y6eR8Gp3imtm/view] Afrique Verte, September 2026), overall biomass levels remain below average across the central, western, and eastern zones, contrasted by near-average conditions in the north.

BGD.comment: In Bangladesh, prospects are very favourable for Aman rice (35% of the country total rice production) to be harvested in November-December as crop biomass is well above average across the country.

BOL.comment: In September, harvests of sorghum (main), maize (minor) and wheat normally conclude before the end of the month. Cropping activities are mainly ongoing in the area of Santa Cruz, the main cereal producing department, where rainfall was 43% below average in the latest month. However average or above average rainfall at the start of the seasons contributed to maintaining good crop conditions throughout the cultivated areas. The prolonged mobility restrictions due to the protests against fuel price increases, among the highest in the region, disrupted supply chains and affected access to food and other essential supplies ([https://share.google/INz3QyspICG24NL26] ReliefWeb). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel, there is a high probability of lower than normal rainfall persisting through the end of the year, especially for the southern western part of the country.

BWA.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops in the main western and southern producing provinces is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_3-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the November–December 2026 period indicates a high probability of below-average precipitation nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with warnings from Botswana's Department of Meteorological Services, which notes that the country faces severe El Niño-driven climate threats. Forecasters warn that the compounding effects of El Niño and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole will heavily strain the upcoming rainy season triggering catastrophic risks for arable farming, extreme risks for livestock, and widespread water shortages ([https://dailynews.gov.bw/news-detail/92605] Daily News). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

CAF.comment: In the southern region, rice and cassava are in the growing stage, with harvests expected to begin in late November. Precipitation in the last 30 days has been recorded 47% below average in Yadé, while in Fertit 35% of the active cropland is seen in poor vegetation status. [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service indicate above-average rainfall during the next months. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/central-african-republic/central-african-republic-situation-report-no-86-22-september-2026] OCHA, persistent insecurity in CAR in September 2026 continued to restrict access to agricultural fields and disrupt farming activities, notably around Tiringoulou in Vakaga prefecture, while in Haut-Mbomou more than 20,000 vulnerable people faced ongoing disruptions to humanitarian assistance after armed men repeatedly blocked and ambushed humanitarian missions.

CMR.comment: The harvest of millet and sorghum in the north will start at the end of September, while the harvest of the main maize crops in the central and southern parts began in mid-August and will conclude at the end of September. Crop conditions are generally good thanks to the average rainfall received since the start of the cropping season. Moreover, rangeland conditions across the country are average to slightly above-average as of mid-September and are expected to adequately support livestock production. However, according to [https://fews.net/west-africa/cameroon/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWSNET (August 2026), ongoing conflict and insecurity across the Far North, Northwest, and Southwest regions continue to drive severe livelihood disruptions, production losses, and persistent Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food consumption gaps among poor and displaced households.

COD.comment: Yam and rice harvests in the north have been completed, while the main-season maize harvest is ongoing in the centre and south. Cassava is currently out of season in the centre and south, whereas in the north it is still in the growing stage. Precipitation has been average across the country over the last 30 days; however, biomass anomalies are recorded in several provinces, with Kongo-Central and North Kivu showing 39% and 31% of their active crop area, respectively, in poor vegetation condition. Water deficits over the last 90 days are widespread in the southern and eastern provinces. The current El Niño episode is expected to favour [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] wet conditions across the country from October, except in the provinces near the Atlantic coast, where a dry outlook is foreseen. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/democratic-republic-congo/cluster-protection-rdc-points-saillants-de-la-situation-de-protection-en-republique-democratique-du-congo-du-mois-daout-2026] UNHCR, recurrent armed clashes and waves of displacement in eastern DRC in August 2026 continued to disrupt people's access to fields, markets and livelihoods, notably in North Kivu's Masisi territory, where nearly 2,980 people fled fighting between 21 and 25 August alone.

COG.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

COL.comment:
In September, the main cycles of maize and rice as well as barley and wheat are normally in the harvesting stage, while minor cycles of maize and rice are in the sowing stage.Rainfall in the past month have been normal to below normal, mostly in the northern departments of the country. Vegetation conditions are normal in most rangelands, likely providing average pasture conditions, while poor vegetation conditions are observed in most cultivated areas of La Guajira and the departments of Cesar and Santander.Fewsnet estimated Crisis (IP Phase 3) level of acute food insecurity classification of La Guajira and the affected area by the August 7.4-magnitude earthquake of Choco ([https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/colombia/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026/print] FEWSNET). According to the 
[https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of the year.

CUB.comment: In September, the main cycle of rice continues in the harvesting stage, while the main cycle of maize has entered the harvest stage.Vegetation conditions remain good, suggesting a correct development of the crop despite the rainfall in the past month has been below average, especially in the Pinar del Rio. However, the problem on the ground mostly hindering agricultural activities, especially the harvest, is the continued shortage of fuel and sanctions to energy companies still in place that are leading to the complete breakdown of many sectors, the agricultural one included ([https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168094] UN). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast normal to wetter than normal conditions, especially in the western part of the country.

DJI.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

DZA.comment: Sowings of next season cereals are expected to start in October under close to or above average rainfall conditions till end November, after which drier than average conditions are expected according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

ECU.comment:
In September, the second cycles of maize, wheat, and barley are in the harvesting stage, while the second rice cycle has finished its vegetation stage. Over the past 30 days, rainfall has been below normal in the eastern part of the country and normal in most cropping areas of the coastal and central provinces. Vegetation conditions are average to above-average, indicating favourable conditions for the development of the minor rice cycle and barley.The latest IPC projections indicate that around 2.6 million people, approximately 15 percent of the analysed population, is expected to face Crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between August and November 2026, with 95.000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Ecuador_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Dic2025_Nov2026_Report_Spanish.pdf] IPC). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast very wetter than normal conditions in the coastal areas with high probability through the end of the year.
 Opposite forecasts are for the central and western part of the country, where conditions are very likely to be drier than normal.

EGY.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

ERI.comment: Despite some mid season rainfall, crop areas in Gash Barka and Debub continued to show below average rainfall in September and rains have generally come late for recovery. The situations looks slightly better in Debub than in Gash Barka. Gash Barka is also the region with most negative impacts on pastoral vegetation.

ETH.comment: Despite some improvement in rainfall in the last 30 days, June to September rainfall in Ethiopia was largely below average in most of the country, with most severe deficits located along the Rift Valley, in Tigray and in Oromo regions. The same regions experienced consistently above average temperatures during the last three months. During the advanced vegetative stadium of the main crop season in Ethiopia (Meher), vegetation conditions from satellite show below average conditions in most of Ethiopia, with strong negative impacts visible in Tigray, in the Rift Valley and Harerge areas, extending southwards into Bale, Arsi and Omo areas. The most severely affected areas are rangelands in Tigray and Gondar, but the impact is visible also in parts of Afar, along the Rift Valley and Bale and Guji areas. Similarly for crops, the worst conditions are observed in the northern part of the country with water deficit impacts extending into the center. The rainfall deficits in the Kiremt season (June-September) had been predicted with the current El Nino conditions and seasonal rainfall forecasts are now pointing towards wetter than normal season in the southern Deyr areas, which might benefit rangeland areas, but also comes with potential floods in areas that have not yet recovered from the 2025 drought. Despite a favourable Belg season in the first part of 2026, concerns over the food security outlook situation are rapidly increasing, driven by the below average Meher season conditions and by rapidly increasing food and fuel prices during the lean season, which continue to erode household purchasing power. The described conditions are of particular concern in a politically instable situation with regional conflicts in Tigray and other areas of the country experiencing new violence.

GHA.comment: In the southern and central bimodal areas, harvesting of the 2026 main-season maize crop concluded in September with average production prospects. At the same time, planting of the second-season maize crop is nearing completion, with mid-month vegetation biomass conditions remaining close to average. In contrast, the cereal harvest in the unimodal north is about to commence, with an expected output ranging from average to slightly below average. This minor shortfall is driven by localized production deficits in the Upper West region, where a negative greenness anomaly affects more than 40% of the active crop area. To a lesser extent, the Northern region is also showing signs of vegetation stress. Meanwhile, pasture biomass conditions across the primary grazing zones of both the north and center remain stable, staying at near-average to slightly above-average levels.

GIN.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 paddy rice crop, the country's main cereal, alongside coarse grains like maize, millet, and sorghum, is expected to begin in October. Rainfall fluctuated from slightly above-average (late May to mid-July) to slightly below-average (late July to mid-August) before stabilizing at average levels by mid-September. Although rainfall distribution has been slightly irregular since the start of the season, crop and rangeland biomass conditions remained average as of mid-September. The only exceptions are the eastern regions of Kankan and Nzérékoré, where a greenness anomaly has affected approximately 25 percent of the active crop area.

GMB.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 maize crop began in September, whereas the harvests of rice and millet are scheduled to commence in October. As of mid-September, crop biomass conditions are at an average to slightly above-average level, pointing to a favourable output for the 2026 season. Moreover, good pastoral biomass conditions are expected to adequately sustain livestock production. According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=GMB] FAO GIEWS (22/09), the government successfully mitigated the impact of high international fertilizer prices and global supply chain disruptions by maintaining the previous year's subsidy levels for the 2026 cropping season, alongside distributing free organic fertilizer and seeds to bolster national cereal production.

GNB.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

GTM.comment: In September, primera cycle crops (Maize and Beans) are normally in harvesting stage. Postrera crops should finish the sowing stage.Effects of El Nino induced drought are particularly strongly felt in the vulnerable Dry Corridor areas, with below average rainfall in the past three months and higher than normal temperatures that has led to planting delays at the beginning of the season and poor crop conditions.In addition, the country is among the hardest hit by the increase in price of fuel, with around +47% year on year change. The latest IPC projections indicate that around 3.2 million people, approximately 17 percent of the analysed population, were expected to face Crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between July and September 2026, with 197 000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165394/?iso3=GTM] IPC). The Government of Guatemala has announced the implementation an action plan against drought caused by the El Niño weather phenomenon ([https://www.latinnews.com/component/k2/item/111486.html?archive=3&Itemid=6&cat_id=840096:in-brief-guatemala-unveils-action-plan-to-address-drought-impact] LatinNews).

HND.comment:
In September, the primera cycle of maize and beans normally enters the harvest stage at the end of the month. The cycle of sorghum and main cycle of rice are in the vegetation stage. The postrera cycle of maize and beans should normally be in the sowing stage. 
Rainfall in the past three months have been below average, in particular in the Dry Corridor areas and the southern part of the country. The drought associated with the El Niño phenomenon led to poor crop conditions in most cropping areas and to declaration of Red Alert for 75 municipalities by the Secretary of State in the Offices of Risk Management and National Contingencies ([https://copeco.gob.hn/] COPECO).The situation is further exacerbated by the increase in fuel prices, among the higher in the region with over 40% year on year change and almost 8% from last month. The last IPC analysis indicated that 1.9 million people were in IPC Phase 3 or above between August and November 2026, including over 104.000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165450/?iso3=HND] IPC). Prospects are not favourable for the entire second cycle of crops as, according to the 
[https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, as there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of the year.

HTI.comment: In September, rice (main cycle) should normally enter the harvesting stage and maize (second cycle) continue the vegetation stage.In the last month, rainfall in cropland areas has been normal across most of the country, benefiting the cycles in sowing and vegetation stage, mostly in the grain producing area of Artibonite. Above average rainfall was received in the northern part while the Sud and Ouest departments received less than normal. Despite erratic precipitations, vegetation conditions are normal to above normal in most cropland areas, mostly supported by the irrigation system, which suggests good harvest prospects for the printemps cycle and the installation of the etè cycle.Despite the positive prospect, the entire food system and supply chain continues to be heavily strained by the insecurity situation in the country and high fuel prices.The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=north_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, it’s more likely that conditions will be direr than normal throughout the end of November but starting to become normal or even wetter than normal towards the end of the year and beginning of 2027. Currently, estimates point at up to 3.9 million of people in need of urgent food assistance during this month ([https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/haiti] FEWSNET).

IDN.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

IRN.comment: In Iran, sowings of winter wheat and barley are underway under very favourable rainfall conditions (till February) according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. As for rice production, harvest finalized with average to above average prospects in the north (Gilan, Mazandaran and Golestan) as well as in Khuzestan but not in Fars. According to Eqtesad-e Moaser (quoted in FAO crop prospects and food situation report), rice production is forecast at 3.9 million tons, as in 2025 and 8% above the 2021-2025 average.

IRQ.comment: In Iraq, sowings of winter barley and wheat are expected to start in October and November respectively under very favourable rainfall conditions (till February) according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. In southern Iraq, harvest of early-maturing rice strains has started with average (Qadissiya) to above average (Najaf) prospects.

KAZ.comment: In Kazakhstan, harvest of spring wheat and barley is nearing completion with very good prospects as favourable rainfall and above average temperature conditions resulted in well above average biomass in all regions except minor producing regions in the centre of the country, namely Karaganda and Abay regions. Sowings of winter wheat should start in the south in October under wetter than average conditions according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. This expectation is consistent with the recognised influence of an El Niño event, which is usually associated with an increase in the autumn‑winter rainfall over Central Asia. Moreover, the current ENSO outlook indicates a very strong El Niño for the September 2026‑January 2027 period, further supporting the forecasted wetter conditions in Central Asia.

KEN.comment: Poor crop production is expected across Kenya’s North Rift and parts of western Kenya following prolonged dry spells and severe rainfall deficits during critical crop-development stages. [https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/fews.net/east-africa/kenya/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com__;!!DOxrgLBm!GvWpxNNoS3o2bepAZH_wm1CK821qFcTUlevYiAwCBQeeT2zfJo6y8aXbCUtXWXbk7FEwl4O3dKctNya28rzaGf7GTIYHLqrggBGJ$" target="_blank] FEWSNET estimates long-rains maize production at 22–28% below the five-year average nationally, with production in key North Rift counties including Uasin Gishu, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Nandi and Trans Nzoia estimated at around 43% below the five-year average. Government assessments also report widespread crop failure in the North Rift, with significant losses reported in Uasin Gishu, Trans Nzoia, Bungoma and parts of Kakamega. The Government has subsequently announced plans to import 25 million bags of maize to address the anticipated national supply deficit. Looking ahead, forecasts of a strong El Niño for the upcoming short rains season point to above average rainfall. It is important however to bear in mind that high intensity rainfall will not be immediately beneficial to drought affected crop areas and that there is a high risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding. These conditions could further affect agricultural production, disrupt livelihoods, and complicate recovery efforts in areas already impacted by the current dry spell.

KGZ.comment: In Kyrgyzstan, harvest of spring cereals and summer crops is underway and prospects are good thanks to above average crop biomass across the country. Sowings of winter wheat should start in October under under wetter than average conditions according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. This expectation is consistent with the recognised influence of an El Niño event, which usually corresponds to an increase in the autumn‑winter rainfall over Central Asia. Moreover, the current ENSO outlook indicates a very strong El Niño for the September 2026‑January 2027 period, further supporting the forecasted wetter conditions in Central Asia.

KHM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LAO.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LBR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LBY.comment: In Libya, sowings of winter cereals are expected to start in October under favorable rainfall conditions till end November, after which drier than average conditions are expected according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

LKA.comment: In Sri Lanka, harvest of second season (Yala) rice and maize completed with good prospects thanks to above average crop biomass in the main producing provinces as a result of a good start of season. Since August, temperatures have been 1-2C above average and a large part of the country, in particular the northern half, received well below average rainfall from 10 August to 10 September, but these dry conditions related to El Niño occurred at the end of the rice and maize cycles.

LSO.comment: Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://fews.net/southern-africa/lesotho/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026) report, which warns that a projected El Niño event will trigger a late and below-average start to the rainy season, which is expected to delay land preparation, hamper early crop establishment, and restrict agricultural labor opportunities. Given these compounding factors, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

MAR.comment: In Morocco, sowings of winter cereals are expected to start in November, under close to average rainfall conditions according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

MDG.comment: In Madagascar, apart from areas where secondary rice is growing, there are no cereals growing now and in the central and northern areas, the next rice season is expected to start in November with the arrival of the rainy season, which is forecast drier than average in the west in November and December and across the country in January by the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.In the Grand South (Anosy, Androy and Atsimo Andrefana), the next cereals and legumes season should start in October under forecast drier than average conditions in the western part (Atsimo Andrefana) from November to February according to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.The Grand South is estimated to have about 1.5 to 2.0 million people facing acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 and above) as a result of extreme events (droughts in 2020, 2021 and 2022, cyclones), poor socio economic conditions and aid reduction according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1161004/?iso3=MDG] IPC analysis [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1161004/?iso3=MDG] and FEWS-NET.

MLI.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 main maize, millet, and sorghum crops began in September, while the rice harvest is expected to start in October. Over the past three months, cumulative rainfall was near to slightly below-average across the primary southern crop-producing zones; however, central and northeastern areas experienced severe deficits. As a result, poor crop conditions are evident in the key producing regions of Ségou, Sikasso, and Koulikoro, where a greenness anomaly affects 40% to 50% of the active crop area. Beyond weather challenges, critical socio-economic factors, such as persistent insecurity, restricted field access, constraints regarding access to agricultural inputs, and population displacement, further threaten overall agricultural output ([https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Z6ICni6evYo_XEyw8_S_y6eR8Gp3imtm/view] Afrique Verte, September 2026). Livestock production faces similar strain: rangeland conditions are below average in Ségou, Tombouctou, and Gao, with 30 to 35 percent of pastoral areas showing vegetative stress. According to [https://fews.net/west-africa/mali/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026), this is compounded by northern and eastern insecurity and restrictions on roughly 30 classified forests in the south and center, which are disrupting traditional migration routes and triggering atypical livestock concentrations.

MMR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

MOZ.comment: Land preparation and planting activities for the main cereal season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_3-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the November–December 2026 period indicates a high probability of below-average precipitation nationwide except for the far northern part where average rainfall conditions are forecast. This grim outlook aligns with reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August), which warn that a projected, very strong El Niño event will cause a delayed start to the rainy season and suppress moisture totals. Consequently, this climate shock is expected to amplify drought risks, trigger poor crop establishment, reduce pasture and water availability, and lower agricultural labor demand across the southern and central regions ([https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August)). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

MRT.comment: Rainfall in the country has been mixed over the last few months, characterized by average cumulative amounts in July followed by well below-average totals from early August to mid-September. Despite this irregular precipitation distribution, both cropland and rangeland biomass conditions remained at average to above-average levels as of mid-September. The primary exception is the Gorgol region, where a greenness anomaly has affected nearly 30 percent of the active crop area.

MWI.comment: Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit across central and southern Malawi, whereas the northern region is projected to receive near-average precipitation. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026) report, which warns that a projected strong El Niño event, expected to persist through at least January 2027, will trigger below-average and poorly distributed rainfall at the onset of the rainy season. Consequently, these compounding climate risks are highly likely to suppress agricultural labor demand, reduce planting levels, hamper crop development, and deteriorate pasture and water availability across the most severely affected central and southern zones ([https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET, August 2026). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

NAM.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops in the main northern producing provinces is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_3-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the November–December 2026 period indicates a high probability of below-average precipitation nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with warnings from the Namibia Meteorological Service and independent forecasters, who note that the country is bracing for a hotter and drier rainy season driven by a strengthening El Niño event starting in October 2026. According to [https://www.namibian.com.na/namibia-warned-not-to-wait-for-el-nino-crisis/] The Namibian, this climate shock threatens to trigger widespread water and food insecurity, slash rainfall by up to 150mm across central and northern regions, and place severe pressure on both the national health and livestock sectors. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

NER.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 main sorghum and millet crops has commenced. Over the past three months, cumulative rainfall was below average in the eastern and central regions, while the western agricultural zones experienced comparatively moderate moisture deficits. Despite these mixed rainfall conditions, overall crop and rangeland biomass conditions remained favourable nationwide as of mid-September. The notable exception is the Diffa region, where a severe greenness anomaly has affected nearly 65% of the active crop area and 55% of the active rangeland area. The country's humanitarian situation is further complicated by severe weather extremes; as of September 14, floods have affected 57,356 people, causing 65 deaths and triggering the collapse of 7,512 houses, with Maradi, Zinder, and Dosso suffering the most significant losses of livestock and food stocks ([https://reliefweb.int/report/niger/afrique-de-louest-et-centrale-derniers-evenements-en-bref-du-15-au-21-septembre-2026] OCHA). Beyond these climate shocks, [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=NER] FAO GIEWS (28/08) reports that civil insecurity continues to restrict field access, particularly in Tillabéri and Diffa, while [https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Z6ICni6evYo_XEyw8_S_y6eR8Gp3imtm/view] Afrique Verte, September 2026 highlights that pastoral conditions remain highly deficient across Maradi, Zinder, and Diffa-.

NGA.comment: In the southern bimodal areas, the main-season maize harvest was completed in August with average production prospects. Planting of the second season maize is expected to be finalized by the end of September and crop biomass conditions so far are average to slightly above-average. In the north, which has only one rainy season, the harvesting of cereal crops has recently started. Crop conditions in the north are close to average thanks to generally good cumulative amounts of rainfall received so far. However, vegetation anomalies are observed across some of the Middle Belt states, as well as parts of the North East and the North West. More specifically Niger, Bauchi, Adamawa, Kaduna and Plateau, are facing a greenness anomaly across approximately 35% to 55% of their active crop area. Similarly, poor pastoral conditions are impacting Niger, Bauchi, Borno and Yobe leaving nearly 30% to 45% of active rangeland affected by a greenness anomaly. According to the latest [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=NGA] FAO GIEWS analysis (16/09), ongoing conflict is restricting farmers' access to land, while high fuel and fertilizer prices are driving up production costs, ultimately leading to reduced planting areas and lower crop yields in the country.

NIC.comment: In September, the primera cycles of maize and sorghum are normally in harvesting stage. The postrera maize and beans (second cycle) and the second cycle of sorghum are in the sowing stage. Rice in the highlands is in the vegetation stage.Cumulative rainfall since the beginning of the primera cycle has been almost a third below average leading to poor vegetation conditions across more than 60% of the agricultural areas in the country. El Nino induced drought is also likely to negatively affect the second cycle of corps. According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very direr than normal throughout the end of the year, which will likely affect second cycle crops development.

NPL.comment: In Nepal, maize harvest finalized with favourable prospects, while rice to be harvested as from October is in good conditions as suggested by above average crop biomass in all provinces.

PAK.comment: In Pakistan, harvest of Kharif maize and rice has started and average crop biomass suggests close to average prospects, thanks to irrigation water and despite low rainfall from 10 August to 10 September in the south likely due to El Niño (Sindh received nearly no rainfall in this 30-day period versus an average of 55 mm, Balochistan received 28% of its normal rainfall and Punjab, the main cereals producing province, received 52% of its average rainfall).

PER.comment:
In September, potato and sorghum cycles are in the harvesting stage while maize cycles should be in the sowing stage.Cumulative rainfall in the past month has been below average in the western part of the country and normal throughout the coastal areas. Nonetheless, the departments of San Martin and Arequipa, important grain-producing department, show poor vegetation conditions likely linked to the excess rainfall and related floods and landslides during the February to April period this year. The sharp rise in fuel price, with almost +64% year on year change, is negatively affecting agricultural activities in the country, leading the government to implement subsidies. In September, the Comisión Multisectorial encargada del Estudio Nacional del Fenómeno "El Niño" maintains an active "Alerta de El Niño Costero", with high probability that the phenomenon persists until Fall 2027 ([https://enfen.imarpe.gob.pe/download/comunicado-oficial-enfen-n-17-2026/?wpdmdl=2161&refresh=6abe72a4878ff1790866084] ENFEN). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecasts a very high probability of wetter than normal conditions in the coastal areas through the end of the year.
 At the same time, conditions are very likely to be normal to drier than normal over the same period in the central and western part of the country.

PHL.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

PRK.comment: In DPRK, maize harvest is nearing completion while rice harvest has started and for both crops prospects are favourable as crop biomass is average to above average in all provinces.

RWA.comment: Season A planting of crops such as sorghum, maize and beans is about to start under below-average rainfall conditions. Iburasirazuba (Eastern Province) recorded no rainfall during the last 30 days, compared with a long-term average of 48 mm. However, Rwanda is forecast to receive El Niño-related above-average rainfall during the October–December (OND) rainy season, as indicated by the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/rwanda/wfp-rwanda-country-brief-september-2026] WFP, the average cost of the food basket in Rwanda rose by 4 percent in August 2026 compared with July and by 9 percent year-on-year, as broader inflationary pressures and high transport and energy costs outweighed the easing effect of recent harvests and further eroded refugees' purchasing power.

SDN.comment: Major rainfall deficits and above average temperatures are characterizing nearly all agricultural areas in Sudan across the 2026 crop season. The season started nearly one month late and experienced drought conditions since its early stages, making below average areas planted and weak crop conditions very likely. The end of September marks 50-60% of crop cycle progress in most agricultural areas in central Sudan, and with the drought conditions experienced so far, it is highly unlikely that crops will recover from stress and failure, making minimal yields are likely. The negative effects on crops and rangelands caused by the rainfall deficits and exceptional heath, come on top of the livelihoods losses and degradation inflicted by the ongoing conflict, characterized by rapid movements of troops, use of drones and continuous displacement. A partial 2026 crop failure will substantially reduce the benefits of green harvest during the lean season and staples availability after harvest, contributing to worsening food availability and access in areas which were already classified as at risk of famine in the latest IPC analysis. This season is substantially different from the previous two years, which have ben charaterized by generally favourable rainfall conditions. Although positive agroclimatic conditions alone were clearly not sufficient to restore rural livelihoods, they have still been supporting local crop and livestock production activities under difficult security conditions and with limited access to farming inputs. On the contrary, the 2026 dry conditions, will further worsen large-scale population displacement and compound the widespread destruction of agricultural assets, infrastructure, and basic services. After more than three years of conflict Sudan is one of the gravest food and nutrition crises globally, with 19,5 Million people affected by high levels of acute food insecurity and several areas at risk of famine as confirmed by IPC in May 2026. The [https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Sudan_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Feb2026_Jan2027_Special_Snapshot.pdf] IPC partial coverage special snapshot update for June–September 2026, covering 56 of Sudan's 195 localities and IDP settlements, identified a risk of famine in 14 areas across North Darfur, South Darfur, and South Kordofan under a reasonable worst-case scenario.

SEN.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 main maize, millet, and sorghum crops began in September, whereas the rice harvest is expected to start in November. As of mid-September, overall crop and rangeland conditions remain average to above-average across most of the country. The primary exceptions are the regions of Kaffrine, Kaolack, Matam, and Sédhiou, where crop development is below-average, with approximately 25% to 30% of the active crop area affected by a greenness anomaly. This below-average crop performance is largely attributed to irregular rainfall distribution within the affected regions.

SLE.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 main rice crop, a staple cereal widely produced and consumed across the country, began this month, while the harvest of minor coarse grains, such as sorghum and millet, is scheduled to start in October. As of mid-September, nationwide crop conditions are near to above-average, pointing to a favourable overall output for the 2026 season. Furthermore, good pastoral biomass conditions are expected to adequately sustain livestock production.

SLV.comment:
In September, the primera cycle of maize is in the harvest stage while the second cycle of bean is in vegetation stage. The main cycle of rice and sorghum are in the vegetation stage. Cumulative rainfall in the past month has been more than a third below average which have hindered the correct development of the crops, especially in the eastern part of the country. Poor vegetation conditions are observed in the 39% of the country and up to 52% of the grain producing areas of San Vincente region. Prospects are not favourable for the entire second cycle of crops as, according to the 
[https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of the year. Fewsnet estimates Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes to be widespread across El Salvador from May to September 2026 ([https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/el-salvador/key-message-update/may-2026/print] FEWSNET).

SOM.comment: Gu 2026 crop production in Somalia was highly variable spatially. Erratic and below-average rainfall affected agricultural production in several areas, particularly in northern and central Somalia. Overall however, Gu production was better than anticipated in southern Somalia ([https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Somalia_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Malnutrition_Jul_Dec2026_Report.pdf__;!!DOxrgLBm!GvWpxNNoS3o2bepAZH_wm1CK821qFcTUlevYiAwCBQeeT2zfJo6y8aXbCUtXWXbk7FEwl4O3dKctNya28rzaGf7GTIYHLq_CyVNX$" target="_blank] IPC estimates indicate that cereal production in southern Somalia was 32% above the 1995–2025 long-term average), while northwestern Somalia's Gu/Karan production was 76% below the 2010–2025 average. For October to December 2026 (Deyr), rainfall is expected to be average to above average, potentially improving pasture and water availability and supporting livestock and crop production. However, El Niño-related heavy rainfall and flooding could adversely affect riverine and low-lying agricultural areas through crop damage, displacement and disruption of market access. The impacts of the poor 2025 Deyr season, including reduced crop and livestock production, continue to constrain household food availability and resilience. Nearly 5.1 million people are facing IPC Phase 3 or above (Crisis or worse) from July–September 2026. This includes 1.4 million people in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) and 3.7 million in phase 3 (crisis).

SSD.comment:
In September, most of South Sudan has experienced below average rainfall, following on earlier months deficits. The impact on vegetation of consecutive dry and hot months has worsened as compared with August and drougth impact on vegetation has expanded especially in the north east and eastern parts of the country. The negative agroclimatic conditions will hamper second season crop planting taking place in October. Also they are expected to have serious negative impacts on livestock conditions, especially where they have persisted for several months now like in East Equatoria, in the central parts of the country and in Upper Nile. Seasonal forecasts from the ICPAC and Copernicus for the Oct-Dec period indicate a high likelihood of close to average rainfall. 
Also, independently from agro-climatic conditions, both farmers and pastoralists are highly vulnerable to the impact of conflict, economic downturn, high influx of refugees from Kordofan and internally displaced population. This scenario is further worsened by the economic effects of the conflict in the Middle East. An estimated 7.8 million people are experiencing IPC Phase 3 or higher (Crisis or worse) according to IPC projection update for the period from April to July 2026. This includes approximately 73,000 in IPC phase 5 (catastrophe), 2.5 million people in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency) and 5.3 million in IPC Phase 3 (Crisis). According to the update, conditions have sharply worsened, with a risk of famine now identified in Luakpiny/Nasir, Ulang, Nyirol, and Akobo, driven by conflict, displacement, and restricted aid access.

SWZ.comment: Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=SWZ] FAO GIEWS (25/08) report, which warns that the prevailing El Niño event poses a downside risk to production through drier-than-average conditions. Close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

SYR.comment: In Syria, sowings of winter cereals are expected to start in October under very favourable rainfall conditions (till February) according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. Food insecurity remains high with about 6 million people in need of food assistance (for a total population of 24 million) according to [https://fews.net/middle-east-and-europe/syria/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWSNET June report, mainly as a result of the economic situation, which affects especially poor households and IDPs (despite favourable weather conditions) and reduction in humanitarian assistance in 2026.

TCD.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 coarse grains and rice crops is underway and expected to conclude by December. Cumulative rainfall from early August to mid-September was well below average across most agricultural areas of the Sudanian and Sahelian zones, compounded by high temperatures. Consequently, crop and rangeland biomass conditions remain suboptimal across the country. Nationally, approximately 45% of the active crop area and 35% of rangeland exhibit a negative greenness anomaly. The regions of Batha, Logone Oriental, Logone Occidental, Ouaddai, and Tandjilé exhibit the largest active crop areas under a significant negative greenness anomaly. Similarly, the five regions with the greatest extent of stressed rangeland are Batha, Wadi Fira, Ouaddai, Sila, and Salamat. According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=TCD] FAO GIEWS (07/09), these climate shocks are severely exacerbated by high domestic fuel prices, restricted fertilizer access, and civil insecurity in Lac Province and the Sudanian zone, all of which are driving up agricultural costs and disrupting farming activities, which is expected to trigger localized production shortfalls.

TGO.comment: Harvesting of the main-season maize crop in the southern and central bimodal areas is nearly complete, with an average output expected thanks to favourable moisture conditions during crop development. At the same time, planting of the second-season maize is underway and expected to be concluded by the end of September, with mid-month crop conditions being at average to slightly above-average levels. In the north, which only has one rainy season, the cereals harvest will begin in October. Despite improved rainfall between late July and late August, pockets of below-average vegetation conditions persist in the northern Kara and Savanes regions. Furthermore, according to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=TGO] FAO GIEWS (28/08), local production prospects in the Savanes region face constraints from a 10 to 20 percent increase in agricultural labour costs, reduced cultivated areas in insecure areas, and elevated prices for agricultural inputs. Nevertheless, [https://fews.net/west-africa/togo/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026) projects that total national production will exceed both the five-year average and the previous season's output.

THA.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

TJK.comment: In Tajikistan, harvest of spring cereals and summer crops finalized with good prospects thanks to above average crop biomass across the country. Sowings of winter cereals should start in October under wetter than average conditions according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. This expectation is consistent with the recognised influence of an El Niño event, which is usually associated with an increase in the autumn‑winter rainfall over Central Asia. Moreover, the current ENSO outlook indicates a very strong El Niño for the September 2026‑January 2027 period, further supporting the forecasted wetter conditions in Central Asia.

TKM.comment: In Turkmenistan, harvest of spring cereals and summer crops finalized and prospects are good thanks to above average crop biomass. Sowings of winter cereals should start in October under very favourable moisture conditions as rainfall is expected to be above average for the next 6 months according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. This expectation is consistent with the recognised influence of an El Niño event, which is usually associated with an increase in the autumn‑winter rainfall over Central Asia. Moreover, the current ENSO outlook indicates a very strong El Niño for the September 2026‑January 2027 period, further supporting the forecasted wetter conditions in Central Asia.

TLS.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

TUN.comment: In Tunisia, sowings of winter cereals are expected to start in October under favorable rainfall conditions till end November, after which drier than average conditions are expected according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

TZA.comment: While most of the country remains in the off-season, rainfall over the past 30 days has been generally average. In the bimodal areas (the northern coastal belt, northeastern highlands, Lake Victoria basin and northern Kigoma), where the Vuli season is about to start, precipitation is [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] forecast to be above average over the coming months as a result of the current El Niño episode, and these conditions could favour crop establishment. However, the T[https://dailynews.co.tz/what-above-average-rainfall-really-means-as-2026-vuli-season-nears/] anzania Meteorological Authority (TMA) warns of possible periods of excessive soil moisture and flooding in these areas that could damage crops and agricultural infrastructure. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/united-republic-tanzania/wfp-tanzania-country-brief-september-2026] WFP, Tanzania's food security situation remains broadly stable thanks to favourable 2025/2026 harvests, with food crop production estimated at 25.2 million tonnes, 6 percent above the previous season. However, food insecurity persists in 14 councils, 13 of which face potential deficits for a second consecutive year.

UGA.comment: Rainfall has been below average in the first two dekads of September in most parts of the bimodal areas, signalling a slight delay in the start of the second crop season. In unimodals areas of Karamoja, poor and inconsistent rainfall from June to August together with high temperatures, a pointer to low harvest expectations. According to [https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/fews.net/east-africa/uganda__;!!DOxrgLBm!GvWpxNNoS3o2bepAZH_wm1CK821qFcTUlevYiAwCBQeeT2zfJo6y8aXbCUtXWXbk7FEwl4O3dKctNya28rzaGf7GTIYHLl0uwfyM$" target="_blank] FEWSNET the increased refugee numbers in Karamoja, together with the poor harvest and high food prices contributes to rapidly increasing humanitarian needs. IPC analysis covering 60 areas estimates that approximately 3.6 million people are experiencing Crisis-level food insecurity or worse (IPC Phase 3+) between July 2026 and January 2027, a 6% increase compared with 2025.

UZB.comment: In Uzbekistan, harvest of spring cereals and summer crops finalized with good prospects thanks to above average crop biomass across the country. Sowings of winter cereals have started under normal (i.e. no rain) conditions but rainfall is expected to be above average from October to February according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. This expectation is consistent with the recognised influence of an El Niño event, which is usually associated with an increase in the autumn‑winter rainfall over Central Asia. Moreover, the current ENSO outlook indicates a very strong El Niño for the September 2026‑January 2027 period, further supporting the forecasted wetter conditions in Central Asia.

VNM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

YEM.comment: In Yemen, in the Coastal Areas, after a delayed start of the Kharif season due to low rainfall in August, conditions of recently sown sorghum and millet are slightly improving thanks to the good rainfall received since mid September. In the Northern & Central Highlands and Southern Uplands, despite mixed rainfall conditions, i.e. below average since July in the east of the highlands (Sana’a, eastern half of Dhamar, Al Bayda) and in the south (Lahj) and closer to average in the central and northern parts of the highlands, biomass of sorghum, millet and summer wheat, to be harvested as from October, is average (mainly in Sana’a) to above average in the central part of the highlands. Food insecurity remains high with about 17 million food insecure people out of 40 million people according to [https://www.wfp.org/countries/yemen] WFP, mainly as a result of the socio economic conditions and conflict.

ZAF.comment: Harvesting of winter cereals is expected to begin in October, with favourable weather conditions throughout the season driving positive production prospects. According to the [https://www.sagis.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/CEC_2026-09-29.pdf] second official production forecast, total winter wheat output is projected at 1.805 million tons, which is close to last year’s level (approximately 5% below). Additionally, 2026 barley production is expected to finish roughly 20% above the 5-year average. Conversely, planting for the main summer cereal season is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_3-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the November–December 2026 period indicates a high probability of below-average precipitation nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://www.weathersa.co.za/api/wp/uploads/2026/09/SAWS-ENSO-Statement-002.pdf] South African Weather Service, which warns that an exceptionally strong El Niño event has formed and is projected to bring severe below-normal rainfall, unprecedented heatwaves, and widespread water scarcity across most of South Africa during the 2026/27 summer season. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

ZMB.comment: Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in late October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zambia/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026) report, which warns that a projected very strong El Niño event will cause a delayed start and below-average precipitation during the 2026/27 rainy season, which are expected to severely reduce planting levels and suppress agricultural labor opportunities. Given these compounding factors, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

ZWE.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_3-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the November–December 2026 period indicates a high probability of below-average precipitation nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zimbabwe/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September), which warn that a projected El Niño event will cause an erratic start to Zimbabwe's November-to-March rainy season and suppress moisture totals. In response to these climate threats, the government approved a six-pillar mitigation plan in September 2026 to stabilize the Strategic Grain Reserve, secure basic food imports, and support national crop and livestock production ([https://farmfutureafrica.co.zw/zimbabwes-six-pillar-super-el-nino-strategy-what-farmers-need-to-know/] Farm Future Africa). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.
